opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real moat, but probably not a permanent one. Post-training right now is pretty complex. It's not just one recipe you can copy from a paper. There's a lot of accumulated know-how: how you collect and filter data, how you set up your reward models, how you balance different objectives so the model is helpful without becoming sycophantic or weirdly verbose, and how you catch regressions. A lot of that is tacit knowledge living in people's heads and in the infrastructure a team has built over years. So companies that have done many iterations do have an edge that's hard to replicate quickly.

That said, I wouldn't overstate it. Some of the lead comes from compute and from having a strong base model, and post-training gains partly ride on that. And knowledge diffuses. People move between companies, ideas leak into papers, and once someone shows that a certain behavior is achievable, other teams can often get there faster, because they know it's possible and roughly what to aim for. You also see people distilling from the outputs of stronger models, which shrinks the gap.

So I'd say better post-training gives you maybe a lead of months, sometimes a bit more, and it compounds if you keep investing in it. You can use your current model to help build data for the next one, and you get feedback from deployment that others don't have. That flywheel is probably the more durable part of the moat. But I don't think any single post-training technique is a secret that keeps you ahead for years.

r002.rationale: It says some post-training lead comes from compute and a strong base model, but does not observe that the companies pursuing the most serious pre-training also pursue the most serious post-training.

r003.rationale: It says distilling outputs from stronger models shrinks the gap, which communicates that output distillation weakens the post-training moat.

r004.rationale: It does not mention using another company’s model as a judge to compare outputs or guide one’s own post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's a pretty meaningful moat, but maybe not in the way people expect. The thing about post-training is that it's not one big idea you can copy. It's an enormous amount of accumulated know-how. You have a lot of pieces that each individually look kind of boring: how you collect the data, how you write the instructions for the labelers, how you set up the reward models, how you handle all the weird edge cases where the model is doing something slightly wrong. And each of those pieces, someone can read a paper and get the gist of it. But getting all of them to work together, at scale, with a particular base model, that's a lot of iteration. So I'd compare it more to something like a manufacturing process than to a single algorithm. There's a lot of tacit knowledge, and it compounds.

The other thing is that post-training is where a lot of the actual product differentiation lives. The base models at the frontier are, at some level, fairly similar. They're trained on similar data with similar architectures. What people actually experience when they use the model, the personality, how it handles ambiguity, whether it does what you asked or something subtly different, whether it's good at coding, a lot of that is post-training. So in terms of what users notice, I think it accounts for a surprisingly large fraction of the differences between labs.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. The moat erodes. The field is small and people move between labs, techniques get written up, and the open models catch up on a lot of this with a lag of maybe a year or so. And there's a bit of a treadmill, where the thing that gives you an edge this year gets absorbed into common practice next year. So I'd say it's a real advantage, but it's one you have to keep earning. It's not like you build it once and sit on it. And the ultimate limiting factor is probably still compute and the quality of the base model, because post-training can only elicit what's already in there. It can shape it and make it reliable, but it's not going to make a weak base model strong.

r002.rationale: It says frontier base models are fairly similar and post-training drives product differences, but does not say that the companies pursuing the most serious pre-training also pursue the most serious post-training.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss distilling another model’s outputs or how that would weaken the moat.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention using another company’s model as a judge to improve post-training.

astra-6.text:
I think it can create a pretty significant advantage, but I’m less sure it creates a durable moat. There’s a difference between having a better recipe today and having something that other companies can’t reproduce over the next six months or a year.

A lot depends on where the improvement comes from. If it’s an algorithmic idea, that might diffuse fairly quickly. If it comes from a really good process for collecting data, figuring out where the model is failing, and iterating on those failures, that’s harder to copy. You have to build the whole process, and there are a lot of details that matter.

There’s also the question of how much of the advantage is visible in the model’s outputs. If another company can train on those outputs, they can potentially recover some of what you’ve done. They might not recover the underlying ability to improve the model further, though.

So I’d probably think of it as a moving advantage. The valuable thing is being able to keep finding improvements, rather than having one particular post-training recipe that stays ahead indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response says a hard-to-copy advantage can come from building a process for collecting data, finding failures, and iterating on them, with many details that matter. This communicates organizational know-how as a source of moat.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare companies’ pre-training efforts with their post-training efforts.

r003.rationale: The response says another company can train on a model’s outputs and potentially recover some of what its creator has achieved, which communicates how distillation weakens the moat.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe using another company’s model as a judge for comparisons to improve post-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it creates a moat, but I’m less sure how durable that moat is. There’s a difference between having a better recipe and having a process that keeps producing better recipes. If you’ve found some trick that gives you a big improvement, other companies can eventually discover it, or find a different trick that gets them to the same place. You probably shouldn’t expect that one result to protect you for years.

The more durable advantage is having a really good research team and a fast experimental loop: you can identify what’s wrong with the model, come up with an intervention, and reliably measure whether it helped. There’s a lot of tacit knowledge in making that work.

And then there’s the question of whether your product gives you access to useful experience that others don’t have. User interactions can tell you what people actually want and where the model is failing, though turning that into a training signal isn’t automatic.

So I’d expect meaningful leads from post-training, but I wouldn’t assume they’re permanent. The moat is more in the ability to keep improving than in any particular post-training method.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss copying model outputs through distillation or how that affects the moat.

r004.rationale: It does not mention using another company’s model as a judge for comparisons.
